text: The Giant's Causeway formed about 50 to 60 million years ago, when [[lava|lava]] flooded the area that is now Northern Ireland. A thick sheet of this hot liquid rock settled in a low basin and cooled slowly. As it cooled, it shrank and cracked into tall columns, most of them with six sides.

Over millions of years, the sea wore away the land, uncovering the columns. Today about 40,000 of them stand along the shore like stepping stones. Some are taller than a two-storey house. The rock is [[basalt|basalt]], the same dark volcanic stone that makes up the Deccan plateau in India.

st.prompt: Why do most columns at the Giant's Causeway have six sides?

options.t: Cooling lava cracks into the shape that uses the least energy
Waves carved them that way
Ancient people cut them into shape

st.reveal: As thick lava cools, it shrinks and cracks. Cracks meet best at about 120 degrees, which naturally makes six-sided shapes, the same way mud cracks when a puddle dries.

d.try: Mix cornflour and water into a thick paste about 2 cm deep in a dish. Leave it in a warm, dry place for a few days. As it dries, it cracks into columns with five, six or seven sides, much like the Giant's Causeway.
myth: The Giant's Causeway was built by giants or carved by people.
The columns are natural. They formed when a thick layer of lava cooled slowly and cracked, around 50 to 60 million years ago. The giant Finn McCool is a much-loved legend.

sec.t:
Around 60 million years ago, Europe and North America were slowly pulling apart as the Atlantic Ocean opened. Huge cracks split the Earth's crust. Lava welled up through them, not in tall cone [[@volcano|volcanoes]], but in floods that spread across the land.

Layer after layer piled up, some of them tens of metres thick. Between eruptions, soil formed and plants grew, and then fresh lava would pour over them. You can still see these red soil layers in the cliffs along the Causeway Coast.

sec.h: Finn McCool and the Scottish giant
sec.t:
Irish legend tells a different story. The giant Finn McCool, or Fionn mac Cumhaill, wanted to fight a Scottish giant called Benandonner. So he built a stone causeway across the sea to Scotland.

In one version, Finn saw how huge Benandonner was and ran home. His clever wife dressed him as a baby. When Benandonner arrived and saw the "baby", he thought, "If the baby is that big, how big is the father?" He fled back to Scotland, tearing up the causeway behind him. Only the two ends were left.

The legend has a geological twist. Across the sea, on the Scottish island of Staffa, Fingal's Cave is made of the same kind of basalt columns from the same lava flows.

In 1986, UNESCO named the Giant's Causeway a World Heritage Site. Hundreds of thousands of people visit each year. Some columns have nicknames: the Wishing Chair, the Giant's Boot and the Organ, a row of tall columns that look like pipes.

Visitors used to take pieces home as souvenirs, so now the site is protected by the National Trust. You can still climb on the lower columns, but people are asked to leave the stones where they lie.

Off the coast near Udupi in Karnataka lie the St. Mary's Islands. They are made of six-sided basalt columns too, but these are about 88 million years old. They formed when Madagascar and India split apart, and lava welled up along the crack.

The Geological Survey of India has made the islands a National Geological Monument. About 20 million years later, India drifted north over a hot spot in the Earth. It poured out the lava that built the [[@deccan|Deccan]] plateau, an outpouring so vast it may have helped finish off the dinosaurs.

text: Most [[@encyclopedias|encyclopedias]] and atlases say the Nile is the longest river in the world, at about 6,650 km. It flows north through eastern Africa and Egypt into the Mediterranean Sea.

But the Amazon in South America is a close rival. Britannica gives it about 6,400 km, yet some scientists have measured it at nearly 7,000 km by choosing a different source high in the Andes mountains of [[@peru|Peru]]. So the honest answer is: probably the Nile, possibly the Amazon. What nobody disputes is that the Amazon carries far more water than any other river.

st.prompt: Which river carries the most water into the sea?

options.t: The Nile
The Amazon
The Ganga

st.reveal: The Amazon carries far more water than any other river, roughly a fifth of all the river water flowing into the world's oceans. It pours out more water than the next several biggest rivers combined.

n.certNote: Most reference books list the Nile as the longest, but some studies measure the Amazon as longer. The result depends on which stream is counted as the true source and where the river's mouth is said to end.

d.try: Measure a wiggly river. Draw a curvy river on paper. Measure it first with a ruler in a few big straight steps. Then lay a piece of string along every bend and measure the string. The second number is longer. Mapmakers face the same problem with real rivers, which is one reason the Nile and Amazon are hard to compare.
myth: Rivers always flow from north to south.
Rivers flow downhill, in whatever direction that is. The Nile flows north, from East Africa to the Mediterranean Sea, and the Ganga flows mostly east, to the Bay of Bengal.
facts: about 6,400 km, or nearly 7,000 km by some measurements

sec.t:
Measuring a river sounds simple, but it isn't. First, you have to decide where it begins. Big rivers are fed by many streams, and choosing which one is the true source can add or remove hundreds of kilometres.

Then you must decide where it ends. The Amazon spreads into a huge mouth, more than 200 km wide in places, mixed with islands and channels. Where exactly does the river stop and the sea begin?

Finally, rivers wiggle. The more closely you follow every bend, the longer the river gets. This is like the puzzle of [[@fractals|fractals]], where a coastline seems to grow longer the more carefully you measure it. Rivers also shift their courses over time.

The Amazon begins as tiny streams in the Andes of Peru, just 160 km or so from the Pacific Ocean, and flows east across South America to the Atlantic. It carries about a fifth of all the river water that reaches the world's oceans.

Its basin holds the largest [[@rainforests|rainforest]] on Earth. In the wet season, the river floods vast areas of forest, and fish swim between the tree trunks. There are no [[@bridges|bridges]] across its main stream. Much of the land around it is forest and swamp, with few roads that would need one.

The Ganga flows about 2,500 km from the Gangotri Glacier in the Himalaya to the Bay of Bengal. The Brahmaputra and the Indus are both longer, each roughly 2,900 to 3,200 km. All three begin in or near the Himalaya and are fed by melting snow and ice, as you can read in [[@rivers-himalaya|the rivers of the Himalaya]].

The Ganga and the Brahmaputra join in [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]] and pour into the sea through the largest river [[@deltas|delta]] in the world.

In the United States, the longest river is the Missouri, at about 3,800 km. It flows into the [[@mississippi|Mississippi]], and together they form one of the longest river systems in the world, roughly 6,000 km from the [[@rocky-mountains|Rocky Mountains]] of Montana to the Gulf of Mexico.

Steamboats once carried cotton, people and goods up and down the Mississippi. The writer [[@mark-twain|Mark Twain]] worked as a river pilot on it as a young man, and later wrote about life on the river in his books.

People sometimes plan [[expedition|expeditions]] to settle the question, paddling or tracking the rivers from source to sea. With satellite images and GPS, the measurements keep improving. For now, most atlases still give the crown to the Nile, while the Amazon wins easily as the biggest river by water.

text: On the International Space Station, astronauts sleep in small private cabins about the size of a telephone booth. Each has a sleeping bag strapped to the wall, a pillow, a laptop and a few personal photos. The astronaut zips into the bag, which stops them from drifting around while they float.

Because there is no [[gravity|gravity]] pulling them down, it doesn't matter if they sleep upright, sideways or upside down. Their body feels the same. But sleep in space has strange problems. The Sun rises every 90 minutes. The station hums with fans and machines. And floating arms drift up in front of the body like a sleepwalking cartoon character unless they are tucked into the bag.

st.prompt: Why must the space station's cabins have fans blowing while astronauts sleep?

options.t: Breathed-out air can collect around an astronaut's head without moving air
Fans stop the sleeping bags from spinning around
Fans help cool the station's computers

st.reveal: On Earth, warm breathed-out air rises and drifts away. In orbit, nothing rises. Air full of carbon dioxide can hang around a sleeper's face. Fans keep air moving so astronauts breathe fresh air all night.

src: NASA, Sleeping in Space; Human Research Program.
Barger L. K. et al. (2014), Prevalence of sleep deficiency and use of hypnotic drugs in astronauts, The Lancet Neurology.
European Space Agency, life on the International Space Station.

d.try: Try a space-style sleep experiment. For one night, keep a notebook by your bed and write down when you fell asleep, when you woke, and how rested you felt, on a scale of 1 to 5. The next night, make the room as dark as possible with a sleep mask or thick curtains. Compare the two.
myth: Astronauts sleep lying down in beds like on Earth.
In orbit there is no up or down, so lying down means nothing. Astronauts zip into sleeping bags fixed to a wall, usually upright, and the bag keeps them in place while they float.
facts: a sleeping bag strapped to the wall of a small private cabin
Sunrises a day on the ISS

sec.t:
The space station circles Earth about once every 90 minutes. That means astronauts pass from daylight into darkness and back again about 16 times a day. If they followed the Sun, they would never sleep properly.

So the station runs on a fixed clock, Coordinated Universal Time, close to London time. Lights are dimmed at "night" and brightened in the "morning". Since 2016, NASA has used special LED lights that change colour, bluer in the morning to wake people up and warmer in the evening to help them feel sleepy. They help keep the astronauts' [[@body-clock|body clocks]] on track.

On Earth, warm air rises. When you breathe out in bed, the used air drifts away. In space, there is no rising and sinking, because nothing is heavier or lighter. Breathed-out [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] can pool in a cloud around your head.

That is why the station's cabins have fans that keep fresh air flowing. Astronauts who forget to switch on the fan can wake up with a headache or feeling short of breath. Noise from the fans is so constant that many astronauts wear earplugs.

NASA plans for astronauts to sleep about 8.5 hours a night. But a big study in 2014 found that astronauts on the space station and the Space Shuttle often slept only about six hours. Excitement, noise, busy schedules and the light show outside all play a part.

Too little [[@sleep-why|sleep]] makes people slower and more forgetful, which can be risky when working with complicated machines. So astronauts track their sleep, and scientists study it closely, partly to plan for long trips to Mars.

A trip to Mars could take six to nine months each way. Scientists are thinking about how to help crews sleep well for years at a time, with better lights, quieter cabins and even better sleeping bags.

India's astronauts will face these questions too. In 2025, Shubhanshu Shukla spent about 18 days on the space station during the Axiom-4 mission, the first Indian to live aboard it. India's [[@gaganyaan|Gaganyaan]] programme plans to send its own crew to [[orbit|orbit]] in a capsule built in India. Wherever they go, astronauts will need to sleep, eat and, yes, use a toilet, each of which in orbit becomes a puzzle, as the story of the [[@space-toilet|space toilet]] shows.

text: The bird with the longest yearly migration known is the Arctic tern. It nests in the far north, in places like Greenland, Iceland, northern Canada and the British Isles. Then, when the northern summer ends, it flies all the way to the seas around Antarctica, and back again the next spring.

Scientists who fixed tiny trackers to terns in 2010 found that the average round trip was about 70,900 kilometres. One tern from the Farne Islands in England, tracked in 2016, flew about 96,000 kilometres in a single year. That's more than twice around the Earth, for a bird that weighs about 100 grams, less than a cricket ball.

st.prompt: Arctic terns fly from the Arctic to Antarctica. Which route do they take?

options.t: A wiggly S-shaped path that follows the winds
The shortest straight line, north to south
Along the coast of every continent

st.reveal: Tracking showed terns zigzag across the Atlantic in a giant S shape. The detours add thousands of kilometres, but they ride helpful winds and stop at rich feeding grounds, which saves energy overall.

src: Egevang C. et al. (2010), Tracking of Arctic terns reveals longest animal migration, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
RSPB (UK), Arctic tern.
Cornell Lab of Ornithology, All About Birds, Arctic Tern.

d.try: On a globe or world map, use a piece of string to trace an Arctic tern's trip from Greenland to the Weddell Sea near Antarctica and back. Then measure your own longest journey the same way. Use the map scale to work out how many of your journeys would make one tern's year.
myth: Birds migrate in a straight line by the shortest route.
Many migrating birds take long, curving routes that follow good winds and food stops. For Arctic terns, the curvy path is much longer, but easier.
facts: about 96,000 km (2016, a bird from the Farne Islands, UK)

sec.t:
Why go so far? Because the tern lives in two summers. When it's summer in the [[@arctic|Arctic]], the Sun barely sets, and the cold seas swarm with small fish. When winter comes in the north, the tern flies south to [[@antarctica|Antarctica]], where it's now summer, with long days and plenty of food.

This happens because Earth is tilted, which is why the [[@seasons-why|seasons]] in the two halves of the planet are opposite. The tern's trick means it probably sees more daylight in a year than any other animal.

Arctic terns are built for flying. They have long, narrow wings and forked tails, like swallows of the sea. They rarely land on water, because their feathers aren't very waterproof. Instead, they hover over the waves, then dive head first to snatch small fish.

They can live a long time. The oldest known Arctic tern was about 34 years old. Add up all those journeys and a tern may fly about 2.4 million kilometres in its lifetime, the distance of three trips to the [[@apollo-moon|Moon]] and back.

On the Farne Islands, visitors walking past tern nests often wear hats. Terns defend their eggs fiercely and dive-bomb the heads of anyone who comes too near, sometimes pecking hard enough to draw blood.

Arctic terns usually lay two eggs in a simple scrape on the ground, with hardly any nest at all. The eggs and chicks are speckled to blend with pebbles and grass. Parents take turns flying out to sea to bring back fish, and the chicks can fly within about a month of hatching. Young terns often stay in the far south for their first couple of years before flying north to breed.

Other birds hold different records. In 2022 a young bar-tailed godwit flew about 13,560 kilometres from Alaska to Tasmania without stopping, in 11 days, the longest non-stop bird flight ever recorded.

India has its own migration marvels. Each autumn, huge flocks of Amur falcons stop in Nagaland on their way from East Asia to southern Africa, crossing the Arabian Sea. Villages that once hunted them now protect them. And the strangest part? Some birds go up instead of across: [[@bar-headed-goose|bar-headed geese]] fly over the Himalayas, where the air is too thin for most people to breathe.

text: A shipwreck is like a time capsule. When a ship sinks, everything on board goes down together: the cargo, the crew's tools, their clothes, their food, even the dice they played with. On land, old things get moved, reused or thrown away. On the sea bed, they often stay right where they fell.

By studying wrecks, [[@archaeology|archaeologists]] learn how ships were built, what people traded, what they ate and how they lived. Some wrecks have rewritten history books. Others answer smaller questions, like what sailors kept in their pockets 500 years ago.

st.prompt: The wooden warship Vasa lay on the sea bed near Stockholm for 333 years and stayed almost whole. Why didn't it rot away?

options.t: The water there is too low in salt for wood-eating shipworms
The ship was painted with a special waterproof paint
Fish kept the wood clean

st.reveal: Shipworms, which are really a kind of clam, bore through wood in most salty seas. The Baltic Sea near Stockholm is too fresh for them. The cold, dark, low-oxygen water also slowed down decay, so about 95 percent of the original ship survived.

src: Vasa Museum, Stockholm (Swedish National Maritime and Transport Museums).
The Mary Rose Trust, History of the Mary Rose.
UNESCO, Convention on the Protection of the Underwater Cultural Heritage (2001).

d.try: Bury a few small, ordinary objects, such as a coin, a pencil, an eraser and a leaf, in a tray of damp sand. Leave it for a week, then dig them out carefully with a spoon, like an archaeologist. Notice which have changed and which haven't, and try to explain why.
myth: Most shipwrecks are full of gold and treasure.

Most ships carried ordinary cargo such as grain, pottery, timber or metal, along with the crew's belongings. To archaeologists, those everyday things are the real treasure, because they show how people lived and traded.
facts: about 3,300 years old, found off Turkey

sec.t:
In August 1628, crowds in Stockholm watched the new Swedish warship Vasa set sail. It was huge, beautifully carved and loaded with cannons. A gust of wind tipped it over, water poured in through the gun ports, and it sank in minutes. It had travelled less than 1.5 km.

In 1961, after years of preparation, engineers lifted it from the harbour. The ship was so well preserved that visitors can now walk around it in a museum built just for it. Studying the Vasa showed exactly why it sank. It was too tall and narrow for its weight, with too little heavy [[ballast|ballast]] low in the hull to keep it upright.

sec.h: Trade routes on the sea floor
sec.t:
Around 3,300 years ago, a ship sank off Uluburun, on the south coast of Turkey. When divers explored it in the 1980s, they found about 10 tonnes of copper, a tonne of tin, blue glass, ebony wood, ivory, gold jewellery and jars of food.

Those goods came from many lands, from Egypt to Cyprus to the Baltic, which supplied [[amber|amber]]. The wreck proved how connected the ancient world was, long before the Romans.

Another wreck changed what we know about science. Off the Greek island of Antikythera, sponge divers in 1900 found a Roman-era wreck. Among its statues was a lump of corroded bronze gears, now called the [[@antikythera|Antikythera mechanism]]. It was an ancient calculator for tracking the Sun, Moon and planets.

{{story:antikythera}}

The English warship Mary Rose sank in 1545 during a battle with a French fleet, as King Henry VIII watched from the shore. When it was raised in 1982, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] found thousands of objects, including longbows, medical tools, combs and shoes. They also found the skeleton of a small dog, nicknamed Hatch, that had probably been kept on board to catch rats. Scientists have even studied the crew's bones and teeth to learn where the sailors grew up.

The [[@titanic|Titanic]], found in 1985 by a team led by Robert Ballard, tells a more recent story. In 2022, searchers found Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance, about 3,000 m below the ice-filled Weddell Sea near Antarctica. It had been crushed by ice in 1915 during an [[@explorers-poles|expedition]] to cross the continent. Its name is still clear on the stern.

Wrecks need protecting. [[@treasure-hunts|Treasure hunters]] have broken up some sites to sell coins and objects, destroying the clues archaeologists need. Many wrecks are also graves, where sailors lost their lives.

In 2001, UNESCO agreed an international convention to protect underwater heritage, encouraging countries to study wrecks carefully and leave them in place where possible. India has also explored the sea for its history, with divers investigating [[@mystery-dwarka|underwater ruins off Dwarka]] in Gujarat and Poompuhar in Tamil Nadu.

text: The oldest known individual trees are Great Basin bristlecone pines, which grow high in the dry mountains of the western USA. One of them, nicknamed Methuselah, has more than 4,800 rings. It began growing around the time the first pyramids rose in Egypt and the cities of the Indus Valley were taking shape.

Some trees are older in a different way. A few clone themselves, sending up new trunks from the same roots for thousands of years. The trunk you see may be young, but the living root system underneath may be far older than any single tree.

st.prompt: How do scientists count a living tree's rings without cutting it down?

options.t: They drill out a thin core of wood, about as wide as a pencil
They X-ray the whole trunk from outside
They measure how tall the tree is

st.reveal: A tool called an increment borer pulls out a straw-thin rod of wood from bark to centre. The rings show up as stripes along it. The small hole does little harm to most healthy trees.

src: US Forest Service, Inyo National Forest, Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest.
Umeå University, Sweden, research on Old Tjikko.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Dendrochronology.
n.certNote: Ages from counting tree rings are reliable. Ages of clonal trees, which regrow from the same roots, are estimates, and scientists disagree about some of them by thousands of years.

d.try: Find a tree stump, a log or a cut branch and count its rings with an adult. Wide rings mean good growing years, narrow ones mean dry or cold years. See if you can find a run of narrow rings and guess what happened those years.
myth: The biggest trees are always the oldest.

Size depends on the species and on growing conditions. Giant sequoias are huge and old, but the oldest single trees known are bristlecone pines, which are short, gnarled and slow-growing, often no taller than a two-storey house.
facts: Oldest known single tree with a ring count
Methuselah, a Great Basin bristlecone pine, more than 4,800 years old
White Mountains, California (exact tree kept secret)
a spruce whose roots may be about 9,500 years old
planted in 288 BCE, the oldest human-planted tree with a known date

sec.t:
Each year, a tree in a seasonal [[climate|climate]] grows a new layer of wood under its bark. In spring the wood is pale and fast-growing, and in late summer it is darker and denser. Together they make one ring. Count the rings from the outside to the centre and you have the tree's age.

Scientists use a hollow drill called an increment borer to pull out a thin core without harming the tree. Ring patterns also record weather. A run of narrow rings means years of [[drought|drought]] or cold. By matching patterns from living and dead trees, researchers have built ring calendars thousands of years long, a science called dendrochronology. These records help scientists reconstruct past [[@climate-change|climates]].

Bristlecone pines live at about 3,000 metres in California's White Mountains, where the soil is poor, the wind is fierce and rain is rare. They grow very slowly, sometimes adding less than a millimetre of width a year. Their wood is dense and full of resin, which protects it from insects and rot.

Many old bristlecones look half dead. Strips of bark die back, leaving bare, twisted wood polished by the wind, while a narrow ribbon of living bark keeps a few branches green. The US Forest Service keeps Methuselah's exact location secret to protect it from souvenir hunters.

In 1964, before these trees were widely understood, a researcher studying ice-age [[glacier|glaciers]] in Nevada cut down a bristlecone with permission from the Forest Service. Counting its rings revealed about 4,900 years. The tree, later called Prometheus, became a lesson in why old trees need protecting.

{{story:redwoods}}

On a mountain in Sweden stands a scraggly spruce called Old Tjikko. Its visible trunk is only a few hundred years old. But scientists dated bits of wood from its root system to around 9,500 years ago, just after the last [[@ice-ages|ice age]]. As trunks died, new ones grew from the same roots.

In Utah, a grove of aspen trees called Pando is really one [[organism|organism]] linked underground, with tens of thousands of trunks. Some scientists think its roots are many thousands of years old, though estimates vary widely.

The oldest tree planted by people with a recorded date grows in Anuradhapura, Sri Lanka. The Sri Maha Bodhi is a sacred fig said to have grown from a branch of the tree in Bodh Gaya under which the [[@buddha|Buddha]] gained enlightenment. According to Sri Lankan chronicles, it was planted in 288 BCE. Gold railings and wooden props now support its old branches, and pilgrims visit daily.

India has very old trees too. The Great Banyan in the botanical garden near Kolkata is more than 250 years old. Its main trunk was removed after disease in the 1920s. Yet it lives on through thousands of [[aerial-root|aerial roots]] that have become trunks, covering an area about the size of a city block. [[@banyan|Banyans]] can spread for centuries this way, which makes their true age hard to pin down.

text: A skyscraper stays up because of three things working together. A skeleton of steel or reinforced concrete carries the weight down through the building. Deep foundations spread that weight into the ground. And the design lets the tower resist, and sometimes soak up, the sideways push of wind and earthquakes.

Weight presses straight down, and steel and concrete are very good at carrying that. The harder problem is wind, which pushes from the side and tries to bend the tower over like a stalk of grass. The taller a building is, the stronger the wind it meets and the more it can sway. So engineers spend much of their effort making tall buildings stiff, well shaped and anchored deep.

st.prompt: The Burj Khalifa is shaped like a stack of setbacks that get narrower as it rises, with three wings. Why?

options.t: To break up the wind so it doesn't push the tower in a steady rhythm
Just to look like a rocket
To make room for more car parking

st.reveal: Wind flowing past a tall tower can peel off in swirls, first on one side and then the other, rocking the building. Because the Burj's shape changes as it rises, the swirls don't line up into one strong rhythm. Its engineers tested models in wind tunnels to get this right.

d.try: Build a tower from drinking straws, paper and tape, as tall as you can. Test it by blowing on it, or by placing it in front of a table fan on low. Then build a second tower with a wider base and criss-crossing straws in triangles, and compare how much each one wobbles.
myth: Tall buildings stand perfectly still.

Skyscrapers are designed to bend a little in the wind, like a tree. The top of a very tall tower can sway by tens of centimetres or more in a strong storm. A tower that couldn't flex at all would be more likely to crack.
facts: steel, reinforced concrete, deep foundations and lifts

sec.t:
Old tall buildings had thick stone or brick walls holding up the floors above. The taller the building, the thicker the walls at the bottom had to be, until there was hardly room inside.

In 1885, the Home Insurance Building in [[@chicago|Chicago]] used a frame of iron and steel to carry its weight instead. It was only ten storeys tall, but its walls no longer had to hold everything up. Many people call it the first skyscraper. Steel frames, along with safe [[@elevators|lifts]], let buildings climb higher and higher. [[@new-york|New York]]'s Empire State Building, finished in 1931, reached 102 floors.

sec.h: A strong spine and deep feet

sec.t:
Wind doesn't just push. As it flows around a tall tower, it can peel off in swirls, first on one side, then the other, rocking the building in a steady [[rhythm|rhythm]]. To stop this, engineers shape towers carefully. The Burj Khalifa gets narrower in steps as it rises, so the wind never finds one steady pattern to push against.

Some towers carry dampers near the top. In Taipei 101, a 660-tonne steel ball hangs on cables. When the tower sways one way, the ball's weight swings the other, calming the motion. Visitors can see it from a viewing floor, painted gold. During typhoons it has been recorded swinging by a metre or more, while the tower around it moves far less.

In places with [[@earthquakes|earthquakes]], such as Japan, California and parts of north India, towers must survive the ground moving beneath them. Engineers design them to bend without breaking, using steel that stretches before it snaps and joints that can flex.

Some buildings sit on rubber-and-steel pads called base isolators. When the ground shakes, the pads move and the building above rocks much more gently. The tallest towers in India are in [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], where dozens of residential towers now rise above 200 metres. Each one has to meet India's earthquake and wind codes before it can be built.

text: A kolam is a pattern drawn on the ground at the entrance of a home, usually in white rice flour. In Tamil Nadu and nearby states, women and girls have done it at dawn for generations. They sweep the doorstep, sprinkle water to settle the dust, and then let the flour trickle from between their fingers into lines, loops and curves.

By the evening, feet, wind and ants have worn it away. The next morning, a new one appears. It is part welcome, part prayer and part art, made fresh every single day. Its northern cousin is [[@rangoli-art|rangoli]].

st.prompt: Why is kolam traditionally drawn with rice flour?

options.t: So that ants, birds and other small creatures can eat it
Because chalk had not been invented
So it glows in the dark

st.reveal: Rice flour feeds small creatures, so drawing a kolam is also a daily act of sharing food. Many women describe it as feeding a thousand souls. Today many people use white stone powder, which lasts longer but isn't food.

They are close cousins. Kolam is the Tamil tradition, usually white line drawings of rice flour made every morning. Rangoli is a wider word used in many parts of India, often for colourful powder designs made for festivals.

sec.t:
Watching an expert draw kolam is like watching someone write very fast in a script you can't read. A pinch of flour is held between thumb and fingers, and the hand moves steadily while the flour falls in an even white line. A large design can take only a few minutes.

Many kolams begin with a grid of dots, called *pulli*. Some designs connect the dots with straight lines into stars and flowers. Others, called *sikku* or *neli* kolams, loop one continuous line around every dot without ever touching them, like a thread wound round pegs. A good sikku kolam often has no beginning and no end.

Kolam isn't only beautiful. It is full of [[@rangoli-symmetry|symmetry]], repeats and rules. In the 1970s, the computer scientist Gift Siromoney and colleagues in Chennai studied kolams. They showed that some could be described by step-by-step rules, the same kind of instructions used in computer programs. A design that looks like art can also be a recipe. Later researchers used kolams to study [[@algorithms|algorithms]], patterns and knots.

A single-line kolam has to obey strict rules: go around every dot, never cross a dot, and close the loop. Kolam artists learn these rules by eye and hand, not by formula, from mothers and grandmothers. Some can draw designs with hundreds of dots from memory.

In crowded cities, many apartment doorways are tiny. Some families now use kolam stickers, stencils or rollers that print a pattern in one go. Others still get up early with a bowl of flour, even on a narrow landing.

Kolam has also spread with Tamil families to Malaysia, Singapore, Sri Lanka and the United States, where it appears at festivals and in school projects about patterns. Artists have drawn kolams on canvas, on walls and in galleries.

And the creatures it was made to feed are still on the job. Watch a fresh kolam for an hour and you may see a line of [[@ants-world|ants]] carrying off the flour grain by grain, back to a nest hidden in the cracks.

text: Recording a song usually happens in four stages. First, musicians record their parts, often one instrument at a time, into [[@microphones|microphones]] or straight into a computer. Next comes editing: picking the best takes and tidying mistakes. Then mixing, where an engineer balances all the parts so each can be heard. Finally mastering, a last polish that makes the song sound good on everything from phone speakers to cinema systems.
Each part sits on its own track. A simple song might have 20 tracks. A big pop song can have more than a hundred, including many stacked layers of the same voice, to make it sound richer.

st.prompt: In most modern pop songs, how are the singer and the band recorded?

options.t: Separately, one part at a time, then mixed together later
All together in one go, like a live concert
The band first, and the singer live on stage later

st.reveal: Most songs today are built in layers. Drums, bass, guitars, keyboards and each line of vocals are usually recorded on separate tracks, often on different days. A mix engineer then blends them into one finished song.

sec.t:
In 1860 a French inventor named Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville recorded someone singing a French folk song, *Au clair de la lune*. His machine, the phonautograph, scratched sound waves as wiggly lines on paper blackened with soot. It could record, but not play back.

In 2008 scientists in the USA scanned those lines and used computers to turn them back into sound. For the first time in nearly 150 years, a ghostly voice could be heard. Meanwhile, in 1877, Thomas Edison had built the phonograph, the first machine that could record a voice and play it back, starting with "Mary had a little lamb".

A recording studio has two main rooms. In the live room, musicians play, often wearing headphones so they hear a steady beat called a click track. Walls are covered in soft panels so the sound doesn't bounce around. In the control room, engineers watch the sound as moving waves on a screen.

Singers usually record in a quiet booth. A round mesh screen, called a pop filter, sits in front of the microphone. It stops the puff of air from letters like "p" and "b" thumping into the recording. A singer may sing the same verse ten times, and the engineer stitches together the best lines.

Mixing is a little like cooking. The engineer decides how loud each part should be and places instruments to the left or right of your headphones. Effects like echo can make a voice sound as if it's in a big hall. Small changes in tone help the drums, bass and voice each find their own space.

Computers have changed everything. In 1997 Andy Hildebrand, an engineer who had used maths to search for oil underground, invented Auto-Tune, which nudges off-key notes into tune. In 1998 the singer Cher turned it up high on purpose, making a robotic sound that's now heard everywhere.

Big studios aren't essential any more. [[@ar-rahman|A. R. Rahman]] built his own studio behind his house in Chennai, where he worked on the music for *Roja* in 1992. In the USA, Billie Eilish and her brother Finneas recorded their first album in his small bedroom, and it won major awards in 2020.

And the strangest part? The microphone, the headphones and the speaker all do the same trick in different directions. They turn wobbles in air into electricity and back, as you'll hear in the story of [[@sound-recording|how sound is recorded]].

text: Mughal miniatures are small, richly detailed paintings made for the Mughal emperors of India, mostly between the 1500s and 1700s. They were painted on paper with [[@art-materials|brushes and bright colours]], often to illustrate books of history, poems and stories.

They were not meant to hang on a wall. An emperor would turn the pages of an album or a book, studying each picture up close. That is why the detail is so fine: a single painting can show every leaf on a tree, the pattern on a carpet and the whiskers on a cat.

st.prompt: In Akbar's workshop, how many artists usually worked on one big painting?

options.t: Often two or three, each doing a different part
Always just one master painter

st.reveal: Many paintings were team efforts. One artist might plan the design and draw the outlines, another added the colours, and a specialist painted the faces. Notes in the margins sometimes record who did what.

d.try: Make a mini painting no bigger than a playing card. Use the finest brush or sharpest coloured pencil you have and fill it with detail, adding a decorated border around the edge. Then look at it through a magnifying glass, the way people once studied Mughal albums up close.
myth: Miniature paintings are called that because the people in them are tiny.

The name comes from their small size and fine detail, meant to be held in the hands and looked at closely. Some Mughal paintings were actually quite large, like the Hamzanama pages, which are about 70 cm tall.

sec.t:
The story begins with the emperor Humayun. After losing his throne in the 1540s, he spent years in exile at the court of the Shah of Persia (modern Iran). There he admired the court painters, and he invited two of them, Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd al-Samad, to join him.

When Humayun won back his kingdom, these artists came to India. They trained Indian painters, and the styles mixed. Persian elegance met Indian colour and storytelling, and later even ideas from European prints brought by traders. The result was something new.

Akbar's son Jahangir had a different passion. He loved animals, birds and flowers, and he kept a diary full of careful notes about them. He asked his painters to record creatures exactly as they looked.

His artist Ustad Mansur painted a zebra sent from Africa, a turkey from the Americas and many Indian birds. A painting of a [[@dodo|dodo]], a bird from the island of Mauritius, is linked to his workshop and is one of the few made from a living bird. Scientists still study it, because the dodo vanished soon after.

The tools were as fine as the paintings. Brushes were made from squirrel or kitten hair, sometimes trimmed to just a few hairs for the tiniest details. Paper was made from cloth fibres, then rubbed with a smooth stone until it was glossy enough for paint to glide across.

The colours, or [[pigment|pigments]], came from minerals, plants and metals. The deep blue was ground from lapis lazuli, a stone brought from Afghanistan. Real gold was mixed into paint or laid on in thin sheets. Painters built up colour in thin layers and polished the surface between them. Some pages took weeks.

As the Mughal [[empire|empire]] weakened in the 1700s, many painters moved to smaller royal courts in Rajasthan and the Himalayan hills. There, [[@rajputs|Rajput]] and Pahari painting grew from the same roots, with bolder colours and many scenes of Krishna. Mughal artists never used strict [[@perspective|perspective]] the way European painters did. They often showed a courtyard from above and the people in it from the side, so you could see everything at once.

text: India has a long tradition of clever arithmetic. Some shortcuts that children learn today are quick tricks for multiplying and squaring numbers, often taught as "Vedic maths". Others come from ancient Indian mathematicians who found brilliant ways to handle square roots, zero and huge numbers.

A famous trick is squaring any number that ends in 5. Take the digits before the 5, multiply by the next number up, then put 25 on the end. So 35 × 35 is 3 × 4 = 12, then 25, giving 1,225. Tricks like this feel like magic, but each one has a solid reason behind it.

st.prompt: Using the "ends in 5" shortcut, what is 85 × 85?
st.reveal: Take the first digit, 8, and multiply it by the next number, 9. That gives 72. Then add 25 on the end to get 7,225. It works for any number ending in 5.

d.try: Practise the "multiply by 11" trick. For 43 × 11, add the two digits (4 + 3 = 7) and put the answer in the middle: 473. Try 52, 36 and 71. Then try 75 × 11, where the digits add up to 12. Work out what to do with the extra 1.
myth: All the tricks in "Vedic Mathematics" come straight from the ancient Vedas.

The book was written in the 20th century by Bharati Krishna Tirtha. Historians have not found its 16 sutras in the Vedas. The tricks work and are fun, but ancient Indian maths is far bigger and older than this one book.

sec.t:
Take a number ending in 5, like 65. It's 60 + 5. When you square it, you get 60 × 60, plus 2 × 60 × 5, plus 5 × 5. That works out to 3,600 + 600 + 25. The first two parts together are always 60 × 70, which is 4,200. So the answer is 6 × 7 hundreds, plus 25.

This is [[@algebra|algebra]] hiding inside a party trick. Once you see why it works, you can invent your own.

Much older Indian maths is just as clever. The Sulba Sutras, written between about 800 and 500 BCE, were manuals for building fire altars of exact shapes. To get the shapes right, priests needed precise [[geometry|geometry]].

[[@baudhayana|Baudhayana's]] Sulba Sutra gives a way to find the square root of 2: 1 + 1/3 + 1/(3 × 4) − 1/(3 × 4 × 34). Work it out and you get 1.4142156. The true value starts 1.4142135. That's correct to five [[decimal|decimal]] places, over 2,000 years before calculators.

In 628 CE, the mathematician Brahmagupta wrote down rules for working with zero and negative numbers. He explained that a number minus itself is zero, and that a debt minus zero is a debt. These rules let people use zero as a real number, not just an empty space.

Indian numerals, including zero, later spread through the Arab world to Europe. The digits 0 to 9 you write today descend from them.

In 1150 CE, Bhaskara II wrote *Lilavati*, a maths book full of puzzles in poetry. One asks about bees: one-fifth of a swarm goes to a kadamba flower, one-third to another flower, three times their difference to a third flower, and one bee is left flying about. How many bees are there? The answer is 15.

Legend says Bhaskara named the book after his daughter, Lilavati. Whether that's true or not, it's still read by students. And India kept producing mental maths stars, like Shakuntala Devi, who in 1980 multiplied two 13-digit numbers in her head in 28 seconds. The record-breaking life of [[@shakuntala-devi|Shakuntala Devi]] began with card tricks she learned as a small child from her father, a circus performer.

text: Dubbing means replacing the voices in a film with new voices speaking another language. Translators rewrite the script, [[@pop-cartoon-voices|voice actors]] watch the film in a studio, and they speak the new lines in time with the actors' lips. Sound engineers then mix the new voices with the original music and sound effects.

Subtitles take a different route. The original voices stay, and short lines of translated text appear at the bottom of the screen. Many films reach the world both ways: dubbed for people who like to listen, subtitled for people who want to hear the actors' real voices.

The colour of the scenery

st.reveal: Viewers notice when a mouth is shut but the voice is still talking, or open when the sound is "m". Translators change words so that lip-closing sounds land at about the right moments, especially in close-ups.

sec.t:
A dubbing studio is a small, quiet room with a screen, a microphone and headphones. The voice actor watches a few seconds of a scene, listens to the original, then records their line. They repeat it until the timing feels right. A director sits nearby, checking that the emotion fits as well as the timing.

Good dubbing artists become famous in their own right. In India, the same artist may voice a [[@hollywood|Hollywood]] superhero in [[@hindi-language|Hindi]] for years, film after film. Children who grow up with dubbed cartoons often know the dubbed voice better than the original.

India has 22 official languages listed in its Constitution and hundreds more spoken every day, as [[@languages-india|languages of India]] explains. So dubbing is big business here. Hollywood films regularly come out in Hindi, Tamil and Telugu as well as English.

South Indian films dubbed into Hindi became huge on TV channels and online, years before they filled cinemas in the north. Some big films, such as *Baahubali*, were shot in both Telugu and Tamil and dubbed into Hindi and Malayalam. This helped [[@cinema-south|South Indian cinema]] reach audiences across the country.

In the 1990s, the Indian researcher Brij Kothari had an idea while watching a Spanish film with Spanish subtitles. What if Indian [[@film-songs|film songs]] on TV showed their lyrics in the same language, word by word? People singing along would practise reading without trying.

His project, Same Language Subtitling, ran with Doordarshan for years on popular song programmes. Studies by the project found that regular viewers improved their reading. The idea has since been tried in other countries.

Countries choose differently. Germany, Italy and Spain have dubbed most foreign films for decades. The Netherlands and Scandinavian countries usually show subtitles, partly because their audiences are smaller and dubbing costs more. Many people there grow up hearing English every day on screen.

Subtitles also matter for people who are deaf or hard of hearing. Captions for them describe sounds too, such as "[door slams]" or "[soft music]". Some streaming viewers now switch subtitles on even in their own language, so they never miss a whispered line.

text: K-pop is popular music from South Korea. Most of it is made by big companies that pick young singers and dancers, train them for years and launch them in groups. Songs are [[@behind-theme-music|catchy]], mix several styles, and come with sharp, tightly rehearsed dance routines and expensive videos.

From the 2000s, K-pop spread far beyond Korea through [[@youtube|YouTube]] and social media. Today groups like BTS and Blackpink fill stadiums in the USA, and K-pop fan clubs meet in cities from Mumbai to Mexico City.

K-pop mixes many styles, including pop, hip-hop, electronic dance music, R&B and rock, sometimes in one song. It is better thought of as a way of making and presenting music, with groups, big dance routines and close ties with fans.

sec.t:
Korean pop songs existed long before, but many people date modern K-pop to 1992. That year a group called Seo Taiji and Boys performed a song mixing rap, rock and dance on a [[@music-reality-shows|TV talent show]]. The judges gave it low marks, but young viewers loved it.

Soon new companies, including SM Entertainment, YG and JYP, began building groups on purpose. They chose trainees, often in their early teens, through auditions. In the late 1990s, Chinese newspapers started calling the spread of Korean pop culture across Asia "Hallyu", the Korean Wave.

A K-pop trainee might spend several years practising before debuting, if they debut at all. Days are packed with singing lessons, dance practice, language classes and fitness training. Many trainees never get picked for a group.

The system has critics. Former trainees and stars have spoken about long hours, strict diets and tough contracts. Some companies have changed their rules after public complaints, and the debate continues.

The training shows on stage. A K-pop group of seven or more members can move in perfect unison, swap positions in a blink and sing live while dancing.

Korean music and TV dramas have been popular in Northeast India for more than twenty years, especially in Manipur, Nagaland and Mizoram. During the 2010s they spread across the rest of the country, helped by streaming and cheap mobile data.

Today Indian K-pop fans run dance cover groups, learn Korean words from songs, and hold contests. Several Indian universities, including Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi, teach the Korean language, and many fans start by singing along to lyrics written in Hangul, the Korean alphabet. The Korean Cultural Centre in New Delhi has run K-pop contests for Indian fans for years.

sec.h: Fans as part of the music
sec.t:
K-pop fans don't only listen. They organise streaming parties to push songs up the charts, design fan chants for concerts, and raise money for charity in their favourite star's name. Each group has an official light stick, so a stadium crowd glows in the group's colour.

That closeness between stars and fans is a big part of why K-pop feels different. Many fans feel they are helping a group succeed, rather than simply watching from the crowd.

text: A few people can swim in water close to freezing because they train slowly for years and their bodies learn to cope. Their first gasp of shock gets smaller. Their blood vessels clamp down harder to save heat for the heart and brain. Many also carry a bit of extra body fat that works like a wetsuit.

They also follow strict rules. They swim for short times, with boats and doctors nearby, and they know the warning signs of danger. For anyone else, icy water is extremely dangerous. This is a sport for trained adults, never something to try alone.

Their blood freezing
Their skin turning to ice

st.reveal: Cold water triggers a gasp and wild, fast breathing called cold shock. It usually passes in about a minute. The safest thing is to float on your back and wait for the breathing to calm before trying to swim.

sec.h: The first minute is the scariest
sec.t:
When cold water hits your skin, your body panics. You gasp without meaning to. Your breathing races, your heart pounds and your blood pressure jumps. This is called cold shock. If your head is under water at that moment, you can breathe in water.

Lifeguards teach the *1-10-1* rule. About 1 minute to get your breathing under control. About 10 minutes of useful movement before your arm and leg muscles get too cold to work. Up to about 1 hour before the body's core cools enough to cause dangerous hypothermia. The numbers are rough guides, but the message is clear: stay calm, float first.

sec.h: How bodies get used to cold

sec.t:
In 1987, American swimmer Lynne Cox swam about 4 km across the Bering Strait, from an Alaskan island to one belonging to the Soviet Union, in water of around 4 °C. It was a swim between two rival countries during the Cold War, and leaders of both praised it.

In 2007, British swimmer Lewis Pugh swam 1 km at the North Pole, in a gap in the sea ice. The water was about minus 1.7 °C. It stays liquid below zero because salt water freezes at a lower temperature than fresh water. In 2015, Indian swimmer Bhakti Sharma swam about 2.25 km in Antarctic waters close to 1 °C. It took her about 41 minutes.

Getting out is not the end. Swimmers can keep cooling for several minutes after leaving the water, as cold blood from the arms and legs flows back to the core. This is called afterdrop. Ice swimmers dress fast in warm layers and sip warm drinks, but avoid very hot showers right away, which can make them faint.

Signs of serious cold include confused speech, clumsy hands and shivering that suddenly stops. Ice swimming clubs make sure everyone watches for them. Many people swear a short cold dip lifts their mood, and scientists are still testing why. For now, the safest way to enjoy cold water is with an adult, a lifeguard and a warm towel waiting. Some animals have gone much further than any human. One small North American frog lets most of its body freeze solid in winter. In spring it thaws out and hops away, a trick explained in the story of the [[@power-wood-frog|wood frog]]. The body's own heater, and why [[@body-temperature|37 °C matters so much]], is just as clever.

text: Nobody knows for certain, and scientists still argue about it. What they do know is when dreams happen. Most vivid dreams come during REM sleep, short for "rapid eye movement", when [[@brain-works|the brain]] is almost as active as when you're awake.

Several ideas try to explain why. Dreams may help the brain sort and store the day's memories. They may help us handle strong feelings, such as worry or sadness, in a safer setting. Or they may be a way of rehearsing tricky situations. Some scientists think dreams are partly a side effect of a busy brain making stories out of random signals.
It's quite possible that more than one of these ideas is right.

st.prompt: In a vivid dream you are running fast. What is most of your body actually doing?

options.t: Lying almost completely still
Moving its legs in time with the dream
Shivering

st.reveal: During REM sleep, the brainstem blocks signals to most muscles, so your body lies still while your brain is very busy. Your eyes and breathing muscles keep working. That's why a sleeping person's eyes may dart around under the lids.

src: Aserinsky E. & Kleitman N. (1953) Regularly occurring periods of eye motility, and concomitant phenomena, during sleep. Science 118.
n.certNote: Scientists know a lot about when dreams happen and what the brain is doing. Why we dream is still argued over. Leading ideas include sorting memories, handling feelings and practising for danger, and dreams may do more than one of these jobs.

d.try: Keep a notebook and pencil next to your bed for a week. As soon as you wake, before you get up or talk to anyone, write down anything you remember from your dreams, even a single picture or feeling. Many people find they remember more dreams as the week goes on.
myth: Some people never dream.
Nearly everyone dreams several times a night. People who say they never dream usually just don't remember their dreams. Woken up in a sleep lab during REM sleep, they almost always report one.

sec.h: The boy with wires on his head
sec.t:
In 1953, a young researcher named Eugene Aserinsky was studying sleep at the University of Chicago with his professor, Nathaniel Kleitman. One of his test sleepers was his own eight-year-old son, Armond, with wires taped near his eyes.

Aserinsky noticed that, several times a night, the sleepers' eyes darted rapidly under their lids. When people were woken during these periods, they usually described vivid dreams. This was the discovery of REM [[@sleep-why|sleep]], and it turned dreams into something scientists could measure.

Some people say their best ideas came in dreams. The Indian mathematician [[@ramanujan|Srinivasa Ramanujan]] told friends that the goddess Namagiri showed him mathematical formulas while he slept. Paul McCartney of the [[@beatles-music|Beatles]] said the tune of his song "Yesterday" came to him in a dream, and he worried at first that he'd copied it from someone.

People have puzzled over dreams for thousands of years. The ancient Indian text called the Mandukya Upanishad describes waking, dreaming and dreamless sleep as different states of mind. In 1899, the Austrian doctor Sigmund Freud argued that dreams show hidden wishes. Many scientists today doubt his ideas, though they agree dreams are often linked to feelings.

Many [[mammal|mammals]] and birds have REM sleep too. If you've watched a sleeping [[@dogs-domestic|dog]] twitch its paws and give [[@words-onomatopoeia|soft little barks]], it may have been dreaming. In experiments, rats that learned a maze replayed similar patterns of brain activity while they slept. We can't ask a rat what it saw, of course.

Bad dreams are common, especially in childhood, and having them doesn't mean anything is wrong. Talking about a nightmare with a trusted adult, or drawing it with a new and better ending, often helps it lose its power.

A few people sometimes realise they're dreaming [[@body-sleepwalking|while still asleep]]. This is called lucid dreaming. In sleep labs, some lucid dreamers have even signalled to scientists by moving their eyes left and right in a pattern agreed beforehand.

Dreams fade fast because the brain's memory-making chemistry is turned down during sleep. Unless you think about a dream soon after waking, it slips away. One study found that older people who grew up with black-and-white [[@television-invented|television]] reported more black-and-white dreams than younger people. Even our dreams, it seems, borrow from our [[@memory|memories]].

text: Your lungs are two soft, spongy bags inside your ribs, but they can't move on their own. Underneath them sits the [[diaphragm|diaphragm]], a dome-shaped sheet of muscle. When it tightens, it flattens and pulls down. Your ribs swing up and out a little at the same time. The space inside your chest grows, and air rushes in through your nose or mouth to fill it.
When the diaphragm relaxes, it springs back up, the space shrinks, and air is pushed out. You do this about 15 to 20 times a minute when you're resting, mostly without thinking about it at all.

st.reveal: The diaphragm, a dome of muscle under your lungs, flattens and pulls downwards. That makes more space in your chest, and air rushes in to fill it. The lungs simply stretch to follow.

sec.t:
Air goes down your windpipe, which splits into two tubes, one for each lung. These split again and again into thinner and thinner branches, like an upside-down tree. At the tip of every twig is a bunch of tiny bubbles called [[alveoli|alveoli]].

There are hundreds of millions of them. Each one is wrapped in a net of very thin blood vessels. The wall between the air and the [[@blood|blood]] is far thinner than a sheet of paper. Oxygen slips across into the blood, and [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]], the waste gas your body makes, slips back out into the air. Spread flat, all those bubble walls would cover about 70 square metres, roughly a [[@badminton|badminton]] court.

sec.h: Breathing where the air is thin
sec.t:
Higher up, each breath holds less oxygen because the air is thinner. On the top of [[@mountaineering|Mount Everest]], a lungful carries only about a third of the oxygen it would at sea level. When Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary first reached the top in 1953, they carried bottled oxygen. For years many doctors thought climbing [[@everest-first|Everest]] without it was impossible. In 1978, Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler did it anyway.

People who live high up, such as in [[@ladakh|Ladakh]] or the Andes, have bodies that have adjusted over a lifetime or over many generations. Some of them have bigger chests or blood that carries oxygen differently.

Every day your lungs take in dust, [[pollen|pollen]] and germs. The tubes are lined with sticky [[mucus|mucus]] and millions of tiny hairs called cilia. The hairs beat together like oars, sweeping the mucus up towards your throat, where you swallow it or cough it out.

This system works well, but it can be overwhelmed. Smoke and [[@air-pollution|air pollution]] carry tiny particles that slip deep into the alveoli, where they are hard to clear. That is why cities like Delhi in winter and Los Angeles on smoggy days warn people to stay indoors when the air is bad. A resting adult moves more than 8,000 litres of air in a day, enough to fill dozens of bathtubs.

text: When an athlete gets hurt, recovery usually happens in stages. First comes protection: resting the injured part so it isn't damaged more. Then the body starts healing on its own, laying down new tissue over days and weeks. Last comes rebuilding, when a physiotherapist slowly brings back strength, balance and movement.

The most common sports injuries are sprains, where a [[ligament|ligament]] (a tough band joining bone to bone) is stretched or torn, and strains, where a muscle or [[tendon|tendon]] is overstretched. Broken bones, dislocated joints and head injuries are less common but more serious.
The hardest part is often patience, for athletes and for children who just want to get back to the playground. Going back too soon is one of the main reasons injuries happen again.

options.t: Ice is the most important part

st.reveal: Dr Gabe Mirkin wrote in 2014 that ice may delay healing, because inflammation is part of how the body starts repairs. Ice can still ease pain for a short time. Many doctors now focus more on gentle movement once the first few days have passed.

n.certNote: Doctors agree on gradual rest, rehabilitation and a careful return to sport. Whether ice actually speeds healing is debated, and advice on it has changed since the 1970s.

sec.t:
Healing starts within minutes. Blood rushes to the injured area, bringing cells that clean up damage. This makes the area red, warm and swollen. It feels bad, but this inflammation is the start of repairs.

Over the next weeks, the body builds new tissue. In a broken bone, a soft bridge called a callus forms across the gap and slowly hardens. A simple break in a child's arm often heals in about six to eight weeks, because young [[@bones|bones]] grow and mend quickly. Ligaments and tendons have a poor blood supply, so they can take months.

Doctors check bones with [[@x-rays|X-rays]], and soft tissue with scanners that use magnets or sound waves. Muscles heal fastest of all, because they are packed with blood vessels. A mild strain can feel better within a week or two.

sec.h: The surgery named after a pitcher
sec.t:
Baseball pitchers throw so hard that the ligament on the inside of the elbow can tear. In 1974, the American [[surgeon|surgeon]] Frank Jobe tried something new on a pitcher named Tommy John. He replaced the torn ligament with a tendon taken from John's other arm.

Nobody knew if it would work. Tommy John returned to pitching and played for another 14 seasons. The operation is now so common that it's simply called Tommy John surgery. Doctors worry, though, that young players are throwing too hard and too often, and more teenagers now need it.

In 2019, the [[@sport-science-javelin|javelin thrower]] [[@neeraj-chopra|Neeraj Chopra]] had surgery on his throwing elbow. He missed months of competition and had to rebuild his strength carefully, step by step. Two years later, at the Tokyo Olympics, he won the gold medal.

His story shows the modern approach. Recovery is planned like training. Physiotherapists set small goals, such as moving without pain, then lifting light weights, then throwing gently, before full competition. They also train the muscles around an injury, so that the [[@joints|joint]] is better protected next time.

In 1978, Dr Gabe Mirkin wrote a popular book that gave the world RICE: rest, ice, compression and elevation. For decades it was standard advice. In 2014, Mirkin wrote that ice might actually delay healing by slowing the inflammation the body needs.

Today many doctors suggest a short rest, then gentle movement as soon as it's comfortable, guided by a professional. Head injuries are different: anyone who bumps their head and feels dizzy, sick or confused should stop playing and see a doctor. Science keeps testing its own advice, and in sports medicine that advice is still changing.

text: Biometrics means measuring the body to recognise a person. The word joins two Greek pieces: *bio*, life, and *metric*, measure. A [[biometric|biometric]] system picks a feature that differs from person to person, such as a fingerprint or the shape of a face. Then it turns that feature into numbers.

Next time that person comes along, the machine measures them again and compares the new numbers with the stored ones. If they are close enough, the door opens, the phone switches on or the payment goes through. Nothing has to be remembered or carried, because the key is part of you.

st.prompt: When you open a phone with your finger, what does the phone usually keep in its memory?

options.t: A set of numbers describing your fingerprint's key points
A clear photograph of your fingertip
Nothing at all. It checks with a website every time

st.reveal: Most phones turn the ridges into a list of key points and store that, locked away in a secure part of the chip. A copy of those numbers can't easily be turned back into a picture of your finger.

d.try: Rub a soft pencil on a scrap of paper until it's dark, press your fingertip on it, then press the finger onto a strip of clear tape and stick it on white paper. Do the same for a friend or family member. Look for loops, whorls and arches, and see how many differences you can find.
myth: Identical twins have identical fingerprints.
Twins share their DNA, but fingerprints form in the womb as the skin presses and folds against its surroundings. Those tiny differences give each twin a different set of ridges.
facts: 10 fingerprints, both irises and a face photo

sec.t:
Fingerprints are the oldest example. The ridges on your fingertips form before you are born and stay the same pattern for life, even after a cut heals. Experts sort them into loops, whorls and arches, then look at where ridges split or stop.

The iris, the coloured ring around the pupil, has a pattern of folds and flecks that is even more detailed. Faces are trickier, because they change with age, glasses, beards and light. Some systems also use voices, the [[vein|veins]] inside a palm, or the [[rhythm|rhythm]] of a person's walk.

A good biometric feature has to pass a few tests. It should differ between people, stay steady over the years, and be quick to measure. Fingerprints and irises score well on all of these. Voices change when you have a cold, and faces change as you grow, so those systems need regular updates.

{{story:fingerprints}}

In the 1890s, police in British-ruled Bengal needed a way to sort criminal records. Two Indian officers, Azizul Haque and Hem Chandra Bose, worked out much of a filing system for fingerprints under their boss, Edward Henry. Calcutta opened one of the world's first fingerprint bureaus in 1897.

The method spread to Britain and then across the world. For decades it was called the Henry system, and the two Indian officers who did much of the maths were only properly credited much later.

India now runs one of the largest biometric systems ever built. When someone signs up for [[@aadhaar|Aadhaar]], the 12-digit ID number, they give all ten fingerprints, scans of both irises and a face photo. More than 130 crore Aadhaar numbers had been issued by 2024.

People use it to collect rations, open bank accounts and get a SIM card. In the US, [[@airports|airports]] and passport offices also collect fingerprints and face photos from many travellers. A machine that can match a face in a second makes long queues move faster. Many Indian airports now let passengers walk through gates that check their face instead of a boarding pass.

If someone steals your [[@passwords|password]], you can make a new one. You cannot grow new fingerprints. That's why careful systems never store a plain picture of your finger. They keep a coded summary instead, often locked inside a secure part of the chip.

Machines also make mistakes. Worn fingertips, common among farm workers and labourers, can be hard to read. Some face systems have been less accurate for certain groups of people, a problem explored in [[@face-recognition|face recognition]]. And many people ask who gets to keep these records and for how long, a question at the heart of [[@privacy|privacy]] laws in both India and the US.

text: Some already do. Drones carry blood, medicines and [[vaccine|vaccines]] to hard-to-reach places in Africa and Asia, and in parts of the United States they drop off takeaway food and small shopping orders. But they are still rare, and most parcels will keep coming by van, bike or post for some time.

The trouble is that [[@drones|drones]] can only carry a few kilograms before their batteries run flat. They also need good weather, clear rules about where they can fly, and neighbours who don't mind the buzzing. Drones are best where roads are slow and the cargo is light and urgent.

sec.t:
In 2016 a company called Zipline began flying drones in Rwanda, a hilly country in East Africa where roads twist through mountains. Hospitals running short of blood for an operation can order it by text message. A fixed-wing drone, shaped like a small plane, is launched from a catapult and flies to the hospital.

It doesn't land. It swoops low and drops a box under a [[@parachutes|paper parachute]], then turns back for home. Since then, Zipline has expanded to Ghana, [[@nigeria|Nigeria]], the United States and other countries.

sec.h: How a delivery drone finds you
sec.t:
Most delivery drones fly themselves. They use [[@gps-how|GPS]] to know where they are, plus cameras and other [[sensor|sensors]] to judge height and spot obstacles. A human operator may watch many drones at once on a screen, stepping in only if something goes wrong.

Some drones are quadcopters, with four spinning [[rotor|rotors]], a bit like small [[@helicopters|helicopters]]. They can hover over a garden and lower a parcel on a cable. Fixed-wing drones fly further and faster on the same battery, but they can't hover, so they drop parcels on the move.

A drone must hold up its own weight and its cargo every second it is in the air. Heavier cargo drains the battery faster. That's why most delivery drones carry a payload of only about 1 to 3 kg, roughly a big bottle of water and a packet of biscuits.

Wind and rain make things worse. A strong [[monsoon|monsoon]] gust can push a small drone off course, and water can damage its electronics. So many services pause in bad weather.

Companies in the United States, including Wing, owned by Google's parent company, and Amazon, have run home-delivery trials in towns in Texas, Virginia and California. Some neighbours like the speed. Others complain about noise or worry about privacy and cameras overhead.

Most experts think drones will grow fastest for urgent, light deliveries: a missing medicine, a lab sample, a spare part for a machine. A drone dropping off a whole week's groceries, flying past the windows of a crowded Mumbai or New York street, is still a long way off.

text: A hyperloop is a planned kind of transport. Passengers would sit in a pod that races through a long, sealed tube. Pumps suck most of the air out of the tube, so the pod has almost nothing to push against.

Without air in the way, and with magnets lifting the pod so it barely touches anything, it could in theory reach about 1,000 km/h. That is about as fast as a jet airliner, and roughly three times faster than the quickest [[@bullet-trains|bullet trains]].
So far, though, hyperloops exist only as test tracks a few hundred metres long. Nobody can yet buy a ticket for one.

st.prompt: Why does a hyperloop pod travel inside a tube with most of the air pumped out?

options.t: Air pushes back on fast things, so less air means less drag
Air would make the pod catch fire
The passengers need to breathe special air

st.reveal: At high speed, pushing air out of the way takes most of a vehicle's energy. With the air pressure in the tube cut to about a thousandth of normal, a pod can go much faster on much less power.

sec.h: Why get rid of the air
sec.t:
When you cycle fast, you feel the wind pushing on you even on a still day. That push is called [[drag|drag]]. The faster you go, the harder it pushes. For a train at 300 km/h, most of its energy goes into shoving air aside.

A hyperloop tube would hold air at about a thousandth of normal pressure, a bit like the thin air very high above the Earth. With so little air, drag almost disappears.

The other thing that slows vehicles down is [[@friction|friction]] with the ground. Hyperloop designs borrow from [[@maglev|maglev]] trains and float the pod on magnetic fields, so there are no wheels rubbing on rails.

sec.h: An old dream with a new name

sec.t:
In November 2020 a company then called Virgin Hyperloop gave the first passenger rides, in a 500 m test tube in the Nevada desert. Two employees reached 172 km/h. That was a real step, but a long way from 1,000.

In February 2025 IIT Madras showed off a 422 m test tube on its campus near Chennai, built with support from Indian Railways. Students there have worked on hyperloop pods since 2017. A test centre with a tube of about the same length opened in the Netherlands in 2024.

India came close to a much bigger project. In 2018 the Maharashtra government agreed to study a hyperloop between Mumbai and Pune, promising a trip of about 25 minutes instead of three hours by road. The plan stalled a couple of years later.

Meanwhile some of the big early companies ran out of money. Hyperloop One, the firm behind the Nevada rides, shut down at the end of 2023.

A real hyperloop would need hundreds of kilometres of tube, kept almost airless and dead straight. Steel tubes grow and shrink as the weather warms and cools, and even a small leak lets air rush in.

Then there is the question of people. Passengers would ride in a sealed capsule, probably with no windows, and turns at such speeds would have to be very gentle or riders would feel sick. Getting everyone out safely in an emergency, in a tube with no air, is a puzzle engineers are still working on.

Supporters say these are problems to solve, not reasons to stop. Critics say a fast ordinary train, such as India's [[@vande-bharat|Vande Bharat]] or Japan's Shinkansen, already does the job at a price countries can pay.

text: Mesopotamia was the land between two great rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates, mostly in what is now Iraq. Its name comes from Greek words meaning "between the rivers". Around 5,000 to 6,000 years ago, people there built some of the world's first cities, and began to write.

Mesopotamia was never one country for long. It was home to many peoples over thousands of years: Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians, among others. They gave the world cuneiform writing, written laws, early maths and astronomy, and one of the oldest long stories ever written down.

st.reveal: The Sumerians and later the Babylonians used a counting system based on 60. Sixty splits neatly into halves, thirds, quarters, fifths and sixths. Astronomers kept using it, and that is why we have 60 minutes, 60 seconds and 360 degrees in a circle.

sec.t:
Southern Mesopotamia is hot and dry, with very little rain. But the rivers flooded and left rich mud. Farmers dug canals to carry river water to their fields of barley and dates. Organising all that digging needed leaders, records and workers, and that helped [[@first-cities|cities]] grow.

There was no stone or much timber, so people built with [[@cave-to-houses|mud bricks]]. Each city had a great temple on a stepped platform called a ziggurat. The Ziggurat of Ur, built about 4,100 years ago, still rises above the desert in southern Iraq.

Watering fields in a hot land had a hidden cost. As water evaporated, it left salt in the soil, and over centuries some farms in the south grew less and less.

Some of the earliest known wheels come from Mesopotamia and nearby lands, more than 5,000 years ago. The [[@wheel-invented|wheel]] was probably used first for spinning clay pots, then for carts.

Mesopotamian scribes counted in groups of 60. We still use their system every time we [[@time-measure|tell the time]]. They also watched the sky carefully and recorded the movements of the Moon and planets on clay, helping later [[astronomer|astronomers]].

Around 2300 BCE, Sargon of Akkad conquered many cities and ruled them together, one of the first [[empire|empires]] in history. Later, Hammurabi of Babylon had about 280 laws carved on a black stone pillar over 2 m tall. Some are harsh, such as "an eye for an eye". Others set fair prices and protect widows and children. The pillar now stands in the Louvre in Paris.

Mesopotamians also wrote stories. The [[@myths-flood|Epic of Gilgamesh]] tells of a king of Uruk who searches for a way to live forever. It includes a great flood, and it is one of the oldest stories in the world.

Seals made in the [[@indus-cities|Indus cities]] have been found in Mesopotamian cities such as Ur. Mesopotamian texts talk of ships from Meluhha bringing carnelian beads, timber and ivory. Most historians think Meluhha was the Indus region, which means Indian goods reached Iraq over 4,000 years ago.

The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal later collected thousands of clay tablets in his palace at Nineveh. When the city was destroyed in 612 BCE, the fire baked many of them hard, and that helped them survive to be read today.

text: Subhas Chandra Bose was one of the leaders of India's fight for freedom from British rule. Millions of Indians still call him Netaji, "respected leader". He was brave, impatient and sure that India would only be free if it fought hard for it.

Bose believed the British would not leave just because Indians protested peacefully. During the Second World War he went abroad, looked for help from Britain's enemies, and led an army of Indian soldiers called the [[@indian-national-army|Indian National Army]]. His army did not win, but its story shook the British and inspired Indians everywhere.

st.reveal: Bose grew a beard, dressed as an insurance agent called Mohammed Ziauddin and left by car in the middle of the night. He travelled through Afghanistan and the Soviet Union and reached Germany weeks later.

Most evidence points to a plane crash in Taipei on 18 August 1945. One official inquiry, in 2005, disagreed, and the mystery still fills books and films.
