sec.h: A top student who said no
sec.t:
Bose was born in Cuttack in 1897, the ninth of fourteen children of a well-known lawyer. He was a brilliant student, and as a teenager he was deeply moved by the teachings of Swami Vivekananda. At college in Calcutta he was expelled for a time after a clash with a British teacher. In 1920, in England, he passed the very hard Indian Civil Service exam, coming fourth. That job meant a safe life working for the British government.

Within a year he resigned. He wrote that he could not serve a government he wanted to remove. He came home and joined the [[@freedom-struggle|freedom struggle]], working with the leader C.R. Das in Calcutta. He was jailed again and again, eleven times in all.

Bose was elected president of the Indian National Congress in 1938 and again in 1939. He respected [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] but disagreed with him. Gandhi believed in non-violence and patience. Bose wanted a quicker, tougher push, and was ready to use force.

The quarrel grew, and Bose resigned in 1939. He started his own party, the Forward Bloc. The British, worried about him, put him under house arrest in Calcutta.

In [[@singapore|Singapore]], Bose took charge of the Indian National Army, made up largely of Indian soldiers captured by Japan. In October 1943 he set up a Provisional Government of Free India. It even had a women's regiment, named after [[@rani-lakshmibai|Rani Lakshmibai]] and led by Captain Lakshmi Swaminathan.

His army fought alongside Japan in Burma and northeast India in 1944, but it was forced back. His famous call was "Give me blood, and I will give you freedom."

Bose's choice to work with Nazi Germany and Imperial Japan is still debated. Supporters say he was using his enemy's enemy. Critics point out that both governments did terrible things in the war.

Japan surrendered in August 1945, and Bose is believed to have died soon after when his plane crashed in Taipei. Then the British put three INA officers on trial at the Red Fort in Delhi. The trials caused huge protests across India, and even some Indian sailors in the British navy rose up. Many historians think this helped convince Britain it could no longer rely on Indian soldiers.

India became free in 1947. Bose's birthday, 23 January, is now marked as Parakram Diwas, "Day of Courage". Ross Island in the [[@andaman|Andaman Islands]], where he stayed in December 1943 when he raised the Indian flag at Port Blair, now carries his name.

text: A chariot is a light, two-wheeled cart pulled by horses, built for speed rather than for carrying loads. It appeared around 4,000 years ago, when two older inventions came together: the [[@wheel-invented|wheel]] and the tamed horse.

For about a thousand years, chariots ruled battlefields from Egypt to China. A king in a chariot could cross a plain faster than any soldier could run. Chariots also carried messengers and nobles, raced in front of huge crowds and rolled through stories and holy books. Then horse riders took over, and chariots slowly faded from war.

st.prompt: Early wheels were solid discs of wood. What change finally made fast war chariots possible?

options.t: Wheels with spokes, which were much lighter
Wheels covered in rubber
Bigger wheels made of stone

st.reveal: Spoked wheels weigh a fraction of solid ones. Paired with tamed horses instead of oxen, they turned a slow farm cart into a light, fast vehicle that could race across open ground.

n.certNote: Archaeologists agree that light spoked chariots appeared around 2000 BCE on the steppes near the Ural Mountains. They disagree about exactly when chariots reached India and whether finds like those at Sanauli were horse-drawn chariots or carts.

Horses won't run into a solid wall of people. Most chariots carried archers or spear-throwers who raced along the edges of a battle, shooting and then wheeling away.

sec.h: From ox cart to race car
sec.t:
The first wheels, from around 3500 BCE, were solid planks of wood fixed together into a disc. They were strong but heavy. Oxen pulled them at about walking speed, which was fine for moving grain or stones.

The big change was the spoked wheel. An outer rim, held up by thin wooden spokes, weighs much less than a solid disc. The oldest known examples come from graves near the Ural Mountains, on the grasslands of present-day Russia and Kazakhstan, dated to about 2000 BCE. People there buried chariots alongside the [[@horses|horses]] that pulled them.

The Rig Veda, one of the oldest Indian texts, mentions the *ratha*, or chariot, many times. In the Mahabharata, Krishna drives Arjuna's chariot at Kurukshetra, and their conversation there becomes the Bhagavad Gita.

In 2018, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] at Sanauli in Uttar Pradesh found wooden carts covered in copper, buried in graves about 4,000 years old. Some experts call them India's oldest chariots. Others point out that their wheels were solid and no horse bones were found, so they may have been pulled by bulls. Horses seem to have been rare in South Asia then, and claims of horse bones there from before about 1500 BCE are few and disputed.

Whatever the answer, chariots became central to Indian stories and art. Temple carvings, coins and paintings over many centuries show gods, kings and heroes standing tall in them. The debate goes on, and it connects to bigger questions about the [[@vedic-age|Vedic age]].

sec.h: Racing, temples and the end of an era
sec.t:
By about 900 BCE, armies had learned to fight from horseback. A rider could go where a chariot couldn't, over hills, through forests and across rivers, and chariots lost their place.

They lived on in sport and ceremony, long after generals stopped using them. The ancient Olympic Games held chariot races, and Rome's Circus Maximus could seat well over 100,000 people cheering for their teams. In India, the 13th-century Sun Temple at [[@konark|Konark]] was carved as the chariot of the sun god Surya, with 24 stone wheels and seven horses. The shadows on some of its wheels can be read like a sundial, and every year at Puri, huge wooden chariots still carry Jagannath through the streets.

text: Borobudur is a huge Buddhist monument in Central Java, Indonesia, built about 1,200 years ago. From the air it looks like a giant stone flower or a stepped cake. Each side of its square base is about 123 m long, more than a football field.

It isn't a temple you go inside. Instead you walk around it, level by level, climbing towards the top. The walls of the lower levels are covered in 2,672 carved panels showing stories from the life of the [[@buddha|Buddha]] and from Buddhist teaching. Higher up, the carvings stop. You reach open round terraces with 72 bell-shaped [[stupa|stupas]] and a calm view of green rice fields and smoking volcanoes.

st.prompt: Borobudur is about 35 m tall, but it has no rooms inside. What is in its middle?

options.t: A natural hill that the builders covered in stone
A hollow prayer hall, now sealed shut
The tomb of the king who built it

st.reveal: The builders shaped a hill and then wrapped it in about two million blocks of volcanic stone. That saved a great deal of work. It also means the monument has no inside to explore, only terraces to walk around.

myth: Borobudur was lost in the jungle until a British governor discovered it in 1814.

Local Javanese people always knew it was there, even when it was half buried under ash and plants. In 1814 Thomas Stamford Raffles sent an engineer to clear and survey it, which made it famous in Europe.

sec.h: A book you read with your feet
sec.t:
Pilgrims walk around each level clockwise, keeping the monument on their right. As they go, the panels unroll like a comic strip in stone. The lowest level shows people caught up in everyday wants and troubles. Further up come stories of the Buddha's past lives and his search for wisdom.

At the top there are no pictures at all. Each stupa is a stone lattice, like a bell made of trelliswork, with a seated Buddha statue inside. The climb is meant to feel like a journey from the busy world to a quiet, empty mind.

The panels are also a picture record of life in old Java. They show ships with outriggers, houses on stilts, musicians, markets and farmers with their animals. Historians use them to work out what people wore, ate and sailed in.

{{story:buddha}}

Borobudur was built between about 780 and 830 CE under the Sailendra [[dynasty|dynasty]], kings who ruled Central Java. The builders used grey andesite, a hard stone formed from cooled [[lava|lava]]. They cut the blocks to lock together like pieces of a puzzle, without any mortar. Gutters and about a hundred spouts, many carved as monster heads, carried away the heavy [[tropical|tropical]] rain.

Java at this time was linked by sea to India, China and Sumatra. Buddhist monks, traders and ideas moved along these routes. The great sea kingdom of [[@srivijaya|Srivijaya]], based in Sumatra, had close family ties with the Sailendras. The style of the stupas grew from older Indian monuments like those at [[@sanchi|Sanchi]].

In the centuries after it was finished, Java's rulers moved east and Borobudur was used less. Eruptions of nearby Mount Merapi dropped ash over it, and plants crept across the stones. The villagers living around it never forgot it, though. They knew the hill of carved stones, even if few outsiders came to see it.

In 1814, Thomas Stamford Raffles, the British governor of Java, sent an engineer to clear it. Over the next century, Dutch teams repaired parts of it. Then, from 1975 to 1982, Indonesia and UNESCO took most of the monument apart, fixed its drainage and put more than a million stones back. In 1991 it became a [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage Site]].

Borobudur still faces dangers. When Merapi erupted in 2010, a thick layer of [[@volcano|volcano]] ash coated the monument, and workers spent months brushing it away by hand.

Millions of feet are a danger too. Steps had worn down, and some visitors touched or sat on the stupas. In 2023 Indonesia began limiting how many people may climb to the top each day, and climbers now wear special woven sandals that are gentle on the stone. Every year at Vesak, the festival of the Buddha's birth, monks walk in procession from nearby temples to Borobudur, as pilgrims did more than a thousand years ago.

text: The statue above Rio de Janeiro is Christ the Redeemer, called Cristo Redentor in Portuguese. It shows Jesus with his arms stretched wide, standing on top of Corcovado, a steep [[granite|granite]] peak in the middle of the city. The statue is 30 m tall, about as high as a ten-storey building, and stands on an 8 m pedestal.

It was finished in 1931. Brazil is home to more Catholics than any other country, and for many people the statue is a religious symbol. For others it is simply the sign of Rio, seen from beaches, streets and aeroplane windows.

st.prompt: The statue looks like smooth white stone. What actually covers its surface?

options.t: Millions of small triangular tiles of soapstone
Thick white paint over steel sheets
Big blocks of carved marble

st.reveal: Under the skin is a frame of concrete strengthened with steel. Soapstone is soft, easy to cut and tough in wind and rain, so builders covered the concrete with small triangles of it. Repairers today still have to match the stone when pieces crack.

myth: Christ the Redeemer is the tallest statue of Jesus in the world.

It is the most famous, but not the tallest. Several statues are bigger, including one in Świebodzin, Poland, that is about 33 m tall without its base. Rio's statue stands out because of where it is, on a peak 700 m above the city.

sec.t:
In 1922 Brazil marked 100 years of independence from Portugal. Catholic groups in Rio proposed a giant statue on Corcovado and collected donations from people across the country. The idea was older. In the 1850s a priest had suggested a religious monument on the mountain, but nothing came of it for decades.

A Brazilian engineer, Heitor da Silva Costa, designed the statue and worked out how to build it. A French sculptor, Paul Landowski, made the models, and a Romanian sculptor, Gheorghe Leonida, shaped the face. The style is Art Deco, popular in the 1920s, with simple straight lines and a calm, still pose. From far away, the shape is a cross.

Carrying heavy stone up Corcovado was the hard part. Luckily a small rack railway, with a toothed rail that lets a train climb steep slopes, had run up the mountain since 1884. It carried workers, cement and supplies to the top.

The statue was built around a frame of [[@cement-concrete|concrete]] reinforced with steel, which was still a new way to make [[sculpture|sculpture]]. Workers then covered it with millions of thin, triangular pieces of soapstone. Soapstone is soft enough to cut easily but stands up well to weather. Many of the tiles were glued onto cloth before being fixed in place, and some volunteers wrote names or messages on the backs. The statue was made in sections, with the head and hands shaped separately. Its arms stretch 28 m from fingertip to fingertip, almost as wide as the statue is tall.

Standing alone on a high peak makes the statue a target for lightning. It is hit several times a year, especially in Rio's stormy summer. In 2014, one strike chipped a thumb and a finger.

The statue has [[@lightning-rods|lightning rods]] on its head and arms, with cables that lead the electricity safely down to the ground. Repair teams sometimes abseil down the arms on ropes to replace damaged soapstone.

At night, floodlights make the statue glow above the dark mountain. On special days it is lit in colours, or with images projected onto it, to mark festivals, football matches or causes the city wants to support.

{{story:lightning-rods}}

sec.h: A place for visitors and pilgrims
sec.t:
Today visitors reach the top by the same railway, by van or on foot through Tijuca National Park, one of the largest forests inside a city anywhere in the world. A small chapel inside the pedestal holds weddings and baptisms. Escalators and lifts now carry visitors up the last part of the climb.

In 2007, Christ the Redeemer was voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in a worldwide public poll. It shares that list with the [[@taj-mahal|Taj Mahal]] and the Great Wall of China. Other huge statues have been built since, including the [[@statue-of-unity|Statue of Unity]] in Gujarat, which is about six times taller. But few have a setting like this one, with the ocean, beaches and green hills spread out far below.

text: Nigeria is a large country in West Africa, on the Gulf of Guinea. It has more people than any other country in Africa, well over 20 crore by United Nations estimates. Its biggest city, Lagos, is one of the largest cities on the continent, though the capital is Abuja, a planned city in the middle of the country.

Nigeria is a land of many peoples. The three largest groups are the Hausa and Fulani in the north, the Yoruba in the south-west and the Igbo in the south-east, but there are hundreds more. Together they speak over 500 languages, so English, left over from British rule, is used as a shared official language. Nigeria is famous for its films, its music, its writers, its food and its ancient art.

Biryani

st.reveal: Jollof is rice cooked in a spicy tomato, pepper and onion sauce. Nigerians and Ghanaians in particular tease each other endlessly about whose jollof is better, online, at parties and even between politicians.

myth: Lagos is the capital of Nigeria.
Lagos was the capital until 1991, and it is still the biggest city. The capital moved to Abuja, a planned city built near the middle of the country.
facts: more than 500; English is the official one

sec.t:
Some of Africa's oldest known [[sculpture|sculptures]] come from Nigeria. The Nok culture, in the centre of the country, made striking clay heads with large eyes and carefully styled hair more than 2,000 years ago.

Later, the [[@ancient-africa|Kingdom of Benin]], in what is now southern Nigeria, became famous for brass and bronze plaques and heads made for its royal palace. In 1897, British soldiers attacked Benin City and took thousands of these objects, now known as the Benin Bronzes. Many ended up in [[@museums|museums]] in Europe and the USA. In recent years, some museums have started returning them to Nigeria. Artists in Benin City still use the same [[@bronze-casting|lost-wax casting]] method today.

In the early 1990s, film-makers in Lagos began shooting films cheaply on video and selling them straight to viewers on cassettes. The 1992 film *Living in Bondage* is often named as the start of what became Nollywood. Within a few years it was producing hundreds of films a year. A 2009 UNESCO study placed it second in the world by number of films, behind India's film industries, including [[@bollywood|Bollywood]].

Nigerian music travels too. In the 1970s Fela Kuti created Afrobeat, mixing jazz, funk and Yoruba [[rhythm|rhythms]]. Today Nigerian Afrobeats stars fill stadiums in London and New York, and their songs climb charts around the world.

In 1958, Chinua Achebe published *Things Fall Apart*, about an Igbo village leader whose world is shaken by the arrival of the British. It is one of the most widely read African novels and is taught in schools across the world. In 1986, the playwright Wole Soyinka became the first African to win the [[@nobel-literature|Nobel Prize in Literature]].

Storytelling runs through daily life, in Yoruba [[proverb|proverbs]], Hausa tales and Igbo folk stories. It reflects the country's mix of [[@languages-world|languages]], each with its own songs and sayings.

Food carries stories too. Jollof rice, cooked in a spicy sauce of tomatoes, peppers and onions, turns up at almost every Nigerian party. Nigerians and Ghanaians tease each other endlessly about whose jollof is better.

text: The most expensive foods are usually rare, slow to produce or need lots of handwork. Saffron, picked flower by flower, can cost more per gram than silver. White truffles, smelly [[fungus|fungi]] found underground by trained dogs, sell for thousands of dollars a kilo. Bluefin tuna, beluga caviar and perfect Japanese melons can sell for astonishing prices at auctions.

Some prices are everyday expensive, and some are one-time records made for fun, luck or fame. In January 2026, at Tokyo's first fish auction of the year, a 243 kg bluefin tuna sold for ¥510.3 million, about $3.2 million or roughly ₹29 crore.

options.t: Restaurants pay a huge price for the publicity and good luck of winning it
That one fish has gold inside it

st.reveal: The first auction of the New Year is a celebration. Winning the top fish brings luck and huge publicity, so sushi chains bid far more than the fish's normal value. Most bluefin tuna sell for a tiny fraction of the record price.

sec.t:
Every January, Tokyo's Toyosu fish market holds its New Year auction. The top tuna is a prize that sushi restaurant owners compete to win, partly for luck and partly for the news headlines. The 2026 fish beat the old record of ¥333.6 million, set in 2019.

Bluefin tuna can grow longer than a car and swim across whole oceans. Overfishing made them scarce, and their fatty belly meat, called otoro, is prized for [[@sushi|sushi]]. Ordinary bluefin sells for far less than the record fish, but it's still costly.

sec.h: Red gold from a purple flower

sec.t:
Truffles are fungi that grow underground among tree roots. The rare white truffle from Alba in Italy can't be farmed reliably, so trained dogs sniff them out in autumn forests. In 2007, a 1.5 kg white truffle sold for $330,000 at a charity auction.

Beluga caviar, salted eggs of the beluga sturgeon from the Caspian Sea, is one of the priciest foods by weight. Wild beluga are now critically [[endangered|endangered]], so most caviar comes from farms.

In Japan, fruit is often given as a gift, and perfect fruit sells for huge sums. In 2019, a pair of Yubari King melons sold at auction for ¥5 million. Growers in the town of Yubari, on the island of Hokkaido, judge each melon on its shape, its netted skin and its sweetness. Only the best go to the first auction of the season.

Part of the answer is [[@supply-demand|supply and demand]]: when something is rare and lots of people want it, the price climbs. Part is labour. Vanilla orchids, grown mostly in Madagascar, must each be pollinated by hand with a small stick, because the bees that pollinate it in the wild live only in Mexico and Central America. A worker can hand-pollinate around a thousand flowers a day, and each flower opens for only one morning.

And part is fame. An auction record, a famous chef or a royal story can make a food more desirable than its taste alone would. Spices have always worked this way. Five hundred years ago, black pepper from Kerala was so prized in Europe that sailors risked their lives to reach India for it, which is why it was nicknamed [[@food-pepper-black-gold|black gold]].

text: Milk is food that [[@mammals-rise|mammals]] make in their bodies to feed their babies. A cow, buffalo or goat makes milk after giving birth, in special [[gland|glands]] in her udder. The milk has water, fat, [[protein|protein]], vitamins, minerals and a sugar called [[lactose|lactose]], everything a newborn needs to grow.

Farmers milk the animals once or twice a day, by hand or with machines. The milk is cooled, collected and sent to dairies. There it is usually heated to kill germs, packed, and trucked to shops before dawn. In India, much of it still arrives in a steel can on the back of a bicycle or motorbike.

st.prompt: Milk is mostly water. So why does it look white instead of clear?

options.t: Tiny drops of fat and specks of protein scatter all the light that hits them
Cows add white colour from their bones
Milk has white paint-like powder dissolved in it

st.reveal: Milk is full of tiny floating blobs of fat and clumps of protein. They bounce light of every colour in every direction, and when all colours mix, we see white. Skimmed milk, with less fat, looks slightly bluish.

myth: Chocolate milk comes from brown cows.

All cow's milk is white, whatever the colour of the cow. Chocolate milk is ordinary milk with cocoa and sugar added. In a 2017 US survey, about 7% of American adults said they believed the brown-cow idea.

sec.h: The country with the most milk
sec.t:
India makes about a quarter of all the milk in the world, more than any other country. Unusually, a big share of India's milk, about 44% in 2024, comes from buffaloes. Buffalo milk is thicker and richer in fat than cow's milk, which is why it makes such creamy curd and [[@cheese-paneer|paneer]].

Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh produce the most. In the USA, California makes the most milk, and Wisconsin calls itself "America's Dairyland".

Fresh milk can carry harmful [[bacteria|bacteria]]. In the 1860s, the French scientist Louis Pasteur showed that gentle heating kills many germs, and the idea was later applied to milk. [[pasteurise|Pasteurised]] milk is typically heated to about 72°C for 15 seconds, then cooled fast.

Many Indian families boil milk at home before drinking it, which also kills germs. Watch a pot of milk heat up and you'll see [[@food-science-milk-boil|a skin form on top]]. That is protein and fat cooking at the surface.

Babies make plenty of lactase, a chemical in the [[@digestion-gut|gut]] that breaks down milk sugar. In most of the world, people make much less of it after childhood. If they drink a lot of milk, they may get tummy aches. This is called lactose intolerance.

But some groups whose ancestors kept cattle, in northern Europe, parts of Africa and north-western India, often keep making lactase as adults. It is one of the best examples of a change in human [[@genes-family|genes]] spreading because of food. Curd and cheese have less lactose, which is one reason people everywhere turned milk into them.

Milk has plenty of [[@bones-growth|calcium]], a mineral your body uses to build [[@bones|bones]] and teeth. It also has protein for muscles. That is why it is part of many school meal programmes. People who don't drink milk can get calcium from foods such as ragi, sesame, leafy greens and some pulses.

Milk is also the starting point for a long list of foods: [[@curd-yogurt|curd]], butter, ghee, paneer, khoa and most [[@sweets-india|Indian sweets]]. A few litres of milk on an Indian kitchen counter can become a whole meal by evening.
